paragraphs: O'Connell Street is the main street in Dublin. Many buildings there are empty or old.
Robert Watt is a top civil servant. He will lead a new company to bring the area back to life. The company will start next month.
Watt said most new homes on the street will be small flats with one or two bedrooms. People may live there and move away later when they have children.
He said some people are afraid to go to O'Connell Street at some times of the day. This problem must be fixed. Some architects said families can live in the city centre too.
sentZh: 奧康諾街是都柏林的主要街道。
那裡有很多建築物是空的或老舊的。
羅伯特・瓦特是一位高階公務員。
他將帶領一家新公司，讓這個地區重新恢復活力。
這家公司下個月就會成立。
瓦特說，這條街上大多數新住宅會是只有一或兩間臥室的小公寓。
人們可能會住在那裡，之後有了孩子再搬走。
他說，有些人在一天中的某些時段不敢去奧康諾街。
這個問題必須解決。
有些建築師說，家庭也可以住在市中心。

paragraphs: Most of the new homes on Dublin's O'Connell Street will probably be small apartments with one or two bedrooms, a senior civil servant has said.

Robert Watt spoke at an architecture conference in Dublin at the weekend. He will lead the new Dublin City Development Company, which will start next month. Its job is to bring new life to the city centre.

Watt said the O'Connell Street area has lost its way and needs a new purpose. The plan is to turn empty buildings and derelict sites into homes. He thinks people may live there for some years and then move out when they start a family.

He also said the State should do more to buy and manage land, and not leave big sites to developers. One example is the Carlton site, which has been empty for about 20 to 25 years. Transport Infrastructure Ireland bought it this year.
Watt said many Dubliners are afraid to visit the street at certain times, so antisocial behaviour must be tackled. Some architects at the conference said families can live in the city centre, too.
sentZh: 一位資深公務員表示，都柏林奧康諾街上的新住宅大多可能會是只有一或兩間臥室的小公寓。
羅伯特・瓦特週末在都柏林的一場建築研討會上發言。
他將領導新成立的都柏林市發展公司，該公司下個月開始運作。
它的任務是為市中心注入新的活力。
瓦特說，奧康諾街一帶已經迷失方向，需要新的目標。
計畫是把空置的建築和荒廢的土地改建成住宅。
他認為人們可能會在那裡住幾年，等到成家後再搬出去。
他也說，國家應該更積極地購買和管理土地，而不是把大片土地交給開發商。
其中一個例子是卡爾頓地塊，它已經空置了大約20到25年。
愛爾蘭交通基礎設施局今年買下了這塊地。
瓦特說，許多都柏林人在某些時段不敢去這條街，所以必須處理反社會行為。
研討會上有些建築師說，家庭也可以住在市中心。

paragraphs: The regeneration of Dublin's O'Connell Street is likely to be dominated by one- and two-bedroom apartments, according to the senior civil servant chosen to lead the project.

Robert Watt, a former secretary general of the Department of Health, was speaking at an architecture policy conference organised by the Office of Public Works. He will head the Dublin City Development Company, which is due to be set up next month to deliver priorities identified by councillors and a city taskforce.

Watt said the area had lost its way and needed a different purpose. The company will focus on converting vacant and underused buildings, as well as derelict sites, mainly into housing. He expects many residents to move on once they have children.

He criticised what he called a developer-led approach to large sites, arguing that the State should play a more active role in assembling land. The company will draw up master plans for sites such as the Carlton, which has been empty for up to 25 years and sits above a planned MetroLink station.
Watt also said antisocial behaviour must be addressed, as many Dubliners avoid the street. Several architects challenged the view that the city centre is unsuitable for families.

Robert Watt, formerly the top official at the Department of Health, made the remarks at an architecture policy conference convened by the Office of Public Works. He is to spearhead the Dublin City Development Company, which will be established next month to pursue priorities laid down by councillors and a city taskforce.

Conceding that the thoroughfare had lost its way, Watt said it required a fresh mission. The company will concentrate on repurposing vacant and underused buildings and derelict plots, predominantly for residential use, with many occupants expected to move on once they start families.

Master plans are to be drawn up for sites such as the Carlton, which has lain idle for two decades or more above a planned MetroLink station.
Watt acknowledged that antisocial behaviour deters many Dubliners from visiting. Several architects disputed the notion that the city centre is ill-suited to family life.
